abstract: Evaluating human–AI co-design requires testing whether coding agents can translate real users’ multimodal requests into working application revisions. We introduce Co-Design Bench, a reference-free benchmark of $273$ tasks curated from $37{,}463$ deduplicated queries across $26{,}314$ real user coding sessions. Its two tracks, Multimodal Editing (ME) and Repository Editing (RE), cover localized edits with optional image, audio, video, or document inputs and coordinated repository revisions. Tasks span three capability dimensions: Grounded Understanding, UI Transformation, and Functional Implementation. The tasks pair normalized requests and runnable pre-edit applications with $2{,}331$ hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria. Our judge-then-refute protocol grades criteria using source and browser evidence, challenges positive verdicts with a separate LLM verifier, and audits visual and interaction claims without gold code or target screenshots. Under a shared agentic harness, the strongest of ten model endpoints passes an average of $69.9\%$ of criteria per task but fully satisfies only $26.4\%$ of tasks. All ten endpoints achieve lower criterion completion on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two. Co-Design Bench provides a testbed for studying the gap between partial requirement satisfaction and complete task success under agentic execution for real-user application revisions.

sections.body: The section argues that existing benchmarks cover reference reconstruction, predefined edits, version-history edits, and repository issues, but leave compound revisions from real coding sessions largely uncovered. On 150 WebCompass-edit tasks, switching qwen3.7-plus from single-shot to agentic execution raises mean graded feature completion from 73.6% to 95.1%, so the authors evaluate with iterative tool access. Co-Design Bench contains 273 tasks, curated from deduplicated queries across real user coding sessions, with expert-authored acceptance criteria. Across ten model endpoints, the strongest passes an average of 69.9% of criteria per task but fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Co-Design Bench tests whether coding agents turn real users' multimodal revision requests into working application changes.

sections.body: This section places Co-Design Bench among related work. Reconstruction benchmarks (Design2Code, WebSight-Test, WebRenderBench, IWR-Bench) compare output against reference pages. Editing benchmarks (DesignBench, MT-Web2Code, WebCompass) revise existing artifacts using version pairs, corrupted pages, or predefined operations. Repository benchmarks (SWE-bench, SWE-bench Multimodal, SWE-Lancer) test issues or freelance requests. The authors note that evaluators can show self-preference and benchmark-dependent reliability, and that source presence alone does not establish reachability or correct behavior. Co-Design Bench differs by fixing a bounded revision recovered from a production session and grading hidden criteria without gold code or target screenshots.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior benchmarks cover screenshot reconstruction, predefined edits, and repository issues, but few cover compound revisions drawn from real coding sessions.

sections.body: Each task is a triple of a runnable pre-edit baseline with its containerized environment, an input comprising a normalized request, optional attachments, and retained session history, and a hidden rubric of criteria. Agents edit the application under a shared harness, and acceptance concerns the final state. Tasks come from production queries across coding sessions, which are deduplicated, filtered and ranked, then consolidated into bounded session intervals. Experts refine requests and author criterion-level rubrics. The Multimodal Editing track has 100 tasks with 553 criteria, and the Repository Editing track has 173 tasks with a mean of 10.3 criteria per task. The tasks do not simulate further user feedback during execution.
sections.heading: Co-Design Bench
sections.headline: Each task pairs a runnable pre-edit application with a normalized request, attachments, and hidden expert-authored criteria.

sections.body: The evaluator builds and renders each candidate, then assigns Pass, Partial, or Fail to each criterion from source diffs, rendered pages, and browser traces. A separate verifier challenges Pass and Partial verdicts for stubs, hardcoded outputs, unreachable entry points, and request mismatches. Audits abort evaluation when required renders, screenshots, or browser-action logs are missing. Strict Completion counts Pass only, Graded Completion gives Partial half credit, and Full-Pass Rate counts tasks where every criterion passes. Two frontend experts checked rubric scores for 200 task-model outputs. The authors state that refutation targets unsupported credit and does not establish the correctness of every verdict, and that failure attribution runs only for cases with graded completion below 0.8.
sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol
sections.headline: A judge grades each criterion from source and browser evidence, then a separate verifier challenges positive verdicts.

sections.body: Ten model endpoints run under the same Claude Code harness, with a three-hour limit and a 120-turn cap, on the 273 tasks. Across all tasks, gpt-6-astra leads with mean strict completion of 0.699 and a full-pass rate of 26.4%. Strict-completion rankings correlate across tracks with a Spearman correlation of 0.818, yet Qwen3.8-27B moves from fifth on Multimodal Editing to second on Repository Editing. On repository tasks, those with one or two edit types score 0.654 strict completion, versus 0.591 for three or four types, and every endpoint scores lower on the broader group. The authors describe these comparisons as descriptive rather than isolated causal effects.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Across ten endpoints, criterion coverage runs well ahead of complete delivery, with the top model fully passing 26.4% of tasks.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the benchmark as 273 real-user revisions with runnable starting states and hidden acceptance criteria, spanning localized multimodal edits and coordinated repository changes under one protocol. The strongest model reaches 69.9% mean strict completion but fully satisfies 26.4% of tasks. The authors cite track-specific rankings, edit-breadth differences, and harness sensitivity as places where reliable delivery remains difficult. They state that runnable baselines and criterion-level evidence support analysis of failures in request grounding, change propagation, and final-state verification, and that the benchmark supports comparing future solvers on unmet requirements.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Co-Design Bench offers a shared setting for measuring complete delivery, with runnable baselines and criterion-level evidence retained.

sections.body: The appendix collects supporting material. Appendix A compares single-shot and agentic execution for qwen3.7-plus on 150 WebCompass-edit tasks, where mean graded completion rises from 73.6% to 95.1% and all-pass tasks rise from 49 to 104. Appendix B gives the combined leaderboard and the modality and edit-scope tables. Appendix C rescores kimi-k3 and Qwen3.8-27B with three alternative judges, and absolute graded scores shift by at most 0.053. Appendix D covers execution limits and token accounting, and Appendix E presents representative cases. Appendix F gives dataset composition and the capability taxonomy, and Appendix J details evaluation implementation and failure attribution.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the WebCompass execution-regime comparison, evaluator sensitivity, resource accounting, cases, dataset composition, and evaluation details.
